candidates.title: Pick Autopsy
candidates.pitch: A visitor drafts a deck of about ten cards for a tiny invented deckbuilder, choosing, skipping or trimming at four forks, and a worker then plays that deck ten thousand seeded runs, painting a 100-by-100 field of wins and losses in a blink. The autopsy replays every fork both ways and splits the win-rate change fairly across the four choices, so the visitor sees which pick carried the run, which was a decoy and which quietly cost points, each with an honest error bar. Ranking the forks before the reveal earns an intuition grade, and any pixel replays its run card by card.
candidates.whyNow: Timeless. Deckbuilder folklore (skip rewards, thin the deck, trust the combo) tends to be argued from the runs a player happens to remember, and this page measures it for one invented game with ten thousand runs per fork. Genre backdrop, reported and unconfirmed: Slay the Spire 2 has been in Early Access since 2026-03-05 per the studio's news post.

research.summary: Fan guides for Slay the Spire treat skipping card rewards and trimming starter Strikes and Defends as a deliberate way to keep a deck thin (one guide suggests staying under about 15 cards unless the deck leans on card draw); guides and forums reportedly disagree on the right size, per a blended search summary, so that point is shown as reported. Opening-hand and draw odds follow the hypergeometric distribution (several trading-card math pages). Deck testers say comparing win rates by hand needs far more games than people play. Methods: the Shapley value averages a choice's marginal contribution over all orderings and the parts sum exactly to the total, which for four forks needs only 16 deck variants; common random numbers are the textbook way to compare simulations. Derived by the scout in a throwaway seeded Node prototype of an invented game, not from the web: 10,000 runs took about 0.13 s, a 16-variant batch 2 to 3.5 s, Shapley parts summed to the total in 8 of 8 scenarios, and matched seeds cut variance only 2 to 24 percent for single-card swaps, so accuracy rests on run count.

sources.title: # COMPARING SYSTEMS
sources.snippet: University lecture notes covering common random numbers, antithetic variates and paired intervals for comparing simulated systems.

sources.title: When Does Pairing Seeds Reduce Variance? Evidence from a Multi-Agent Economic Simulation
sources.snippet: A paper shows the variance of a paired estimator equals the unpaired variance minus a term that grows with the covariance between paired outcomes, so the gain depends on correlation.
sources.note: Supports the caution that pairing seeds does not always help, which matches the scout's own measurement. Not opened.

sources.title: Shapley value

sources.note: Establishes the definition and the efficiency property. Result text only; the host cannot be fetched from here.

sources.title: Why did the distribution change?
sources.snippet: A paper states the efficiency axiom (individual values sum to the grand coalition's payoff) and notes that efficiency, symmetry, dummy player and linearity together fix the Shapley value.
sources.note: Third source for the axioms of the Shapley value. Not opened.

facts.claim: Opening-hand and draw odds in card games follow the hypergeometric distribution (draws without replacement); one worked example uses 3 copies in a 40-card deck and a 5-card hand.

As of 2026-10-11, fan guides for Slay the Spire commonly advise skipping most card rewards and trimming starter cards to keep the deck small; one guide suggests staying under about 15 cards unless the deck relies on card draw.
Common random numbers (matched random inputs) are the standard way to compare simulated alternatives, and the variance reduction depends on how strongly the paired outcomes correlate.

The Shapley value gives each choice its average marginal contribution over all orderings and the values add up exactly to the total change (efficiency); for four choices that is 16 deck variants (2^4, counted by the scout).
Deck testers report that comparing win rates by hand needs far more games than people play, because single cards change results only slightly and game variance is high.
A Pokemon testing guide suggests at least 10 to 20 goldfish sessions as a rough convention (single source, unverified).
A university project on card drafting for Slay the Spire exists (single source, findings not seen, unverified).
Slay the Spire 2 launched into Steam Early Access on 2026-03-05 (reported; date read from the post URL; single source, unverified).

design.coreLoop: A visitor meets four forks (three pick-one-of-three-or-skip rewards and one trim-a-card shrine) and builds a deck of about ten cards, after ranking which fork they think will matter most. A worker plays the deck ten thousand seeded runs and paints a 100-by-100 field of wins and losses. The autopsy replays all 16 variants of the four forks, splits the win-rate change fairly across the choices and labels each as load-bearing, decoy or harmful with a 95 percent bar. Flipping any fork repaints the field in a fraction of a second, any pixel replays its run card by card, and the intuition grade makes the second and tenth draft each teach something new.
sophisticationHooks: Exact Shapley attribution over the 16 deck variants of the four forks, parts summing exactly to the total change (verified in a scout prototype), with a 95 percent bar from per-run contributions
Honest uncertainty: binomial error bars, a how-many-runs-would-a-human-need panel, and a measured paired-versus-unpaired variance ratio shown on screen instead of an assumed benefit
Exact hypergeometric overlays (chance a key card is in the opening hand or seen by turn three) beside the simulated frequency so the two visibly agree
Deterministic keyed shuffles: any one of the ten thousand runs replays from its seed, and the URL hash restores the draft, seed and results
design.scopeForOneDay: In one morning the team builds: the invented game (12 to 16 cards, three rooms, fixed greedy autopilot) and its seeded engine with node self-checks (hypergeometric counts, Shapley sum, determinism); the four-fork draft UI; worker batches with progress; the 100-by-100 canvas field with click-to-replay; the autopsy panel with bars and verdict labels; rewind by flipping a fork; the predict-then-reveal grade; an about panel with dated sources; hash state; light and dark; reduced motion. Cut: multiple card pools, relics, multi-act runs, animated fights, sound, daily leaderboards.
risks: The pilot is a fixed greedy autopilot, so every number means this deck under this pilot; the page calls it a ruler, not an oracle, and makes no claim of optimal play.

Balance of the invented game decides everything: in the scout prototype single-card effects ranged from about minus 54 to plus 35 points in a harsh setting and minus 7 to plus 6 in a gentle one, with few near-zero decoys, so the card pool and enemies need tuning until decoys, synergies and traps all exist; a node harness can assert that spread.

Matched seeds were measured to help little (variance ratio 0.76 to 0.98 for single-card swaps in the prototype); the page shows its own measured ratio and relies on 10,000 runs per variant rather than an assumed gain.
A 16-variant batch of 10,000 runs took about 2 to 3.5 s in Node; a browser worker needs a progress bar, a cancel path and a lower run count (for example 4,000) on slow phones.

Unverified items stay flagged: the Slay the Spire 2 Early Access date, the 10 to 20 session rule of thumb, the Edinburgh drafting project and the reported disagreement on deck size each rest on one result or a blended summary, and the page shows them as 'as of 2026-10-11, per the named source' or omits them. Selection bias in pick-rate stats is the scout's own reasoning.
Safety framing: every card, enemy and name is invented, results are labelled simulated, nothing involves money or stakes, and no third-party art or audio is used.

candidates.title: Shuffle Sharp
candidates.pitch: A lazy dealer riffles a fresh 52-card deck once or twice and a visitor, playing the sharp, calls each next card as it turns over. After a single idealised riffle about 31 cards can be called against 4.5 for blind guessing (the scout's seeded count), and each extra shuffle melts that edge until it is near half a card at seven riffles. A feint mode adds false shuffles and perfect faros that only look mixed, and an exact curve shows why seven is the magic number.
candidates.whyNow: Timeless. A famous result becomes something felt in the fingers: exploiting a lazy shuffle is the card-table version of exploiting a strategy that mixes too little, and the curve is the plain-language picture of unexploitable play. In board-game deckbuilders every reshuffle of a hand-shuffled discard pile is a place where order can leak.

research.summary: After k riffles a deck holds only arrangements with at most 2^k rising sequences, and the chance of an arrangement depends only on its rising-sequence count r as C(2^k + n - r, n) over 2^(kn); the scout checked this law by exhaustive enumeration for small decks. Exact 52-card total variation distance (computed by the scout from Eulerian numbers) is 1.000 through k=4, then 0.924, 0.614, 0.334, 0.167, 0.085, 0.043 for k=5 to 10, matching the often-cited rule of about seven riffles (Harvey Mudd, MathWorks, Science News, the Bayer-Diaconis paper). Card guessing with complete feedback after one riffle is studied in several papers; the scout's seeded count for 52 cards gives 31.1 correct for a heads-tracking guesser (an exact Bayes guesser for one riffle matches at 31.2) against 4.5 for blind guessing, then 19.6, 12.9, 8.8, 6.6, 5.5, 5.0, 4.8, 4.7, 4.6 for 2 to 10 riffles. Eight perfect out-faros restore 52 cards (several sources; scout recount agrees).

sources.title: Seven Shuffles

sources.title: how many times should you shuffle the cards 2
sources.snippet: A numerical-computing blog post on how many riffle shuffles randomise a deck; the search summary mentions a computation where total variation falls below one half at seven.

sources.title: bayer diaconis
sources.snippet: A PDF copy of the 1992 paper on the dovetail (riffle) shuffle; its Theorem 1 gives the chance of an arrangement after m shuffles in terms of its number of rising sequences.
sources.note: Primary source for the riffle law. The formula was garbled in the snippets, so the scout checked C(a+n-r,n)/a^n by exhaustive enumeration for small decks. Not opened.

sources.title: Rising Sequences in Card Shuffling
sources.snippet: A fun-facts page defining rising sequences, the maximal runs of cards that keep their original relative order in a shuffled deck.
sources.note: Establishes the statistic that tracks how much order a riffled deck keeps. Not opened.

sources.title: Disorder in the Deck
sources.snippet: A popular article says that with five or fewer shuffles the deck's original order is strongly in evidence, and with more than seven it has virtually disappeared.
sources.note: Independent popular-press confirmation of the five-to-seven range. Not opened.

sources.title: On card guessing game with one time riffle shuffle and complete feedback
sources.snippet: A paper gives an optimal strategy for guessing cards after one riffle shuffle with complete feedback, with maximum expected correct guesses of order n/2 plus a term of order the square root of n.
sources.note: Establishes the game and the single-riffle result; the scout's seeded count for n=52 (31.2 correct) is consistent with it. The same paper appears on other hosts, which are not independent. arxiv.org itself failed to fetch at DNS.

sources.title: The card guessing game: A generating function approach
sources.snippet: A later paper gives an expression for the expected number of correct guesses with an arbitrary number of terms, improving on earlier results.
sources.note: Independent second paper on the same game. Not opened.

sources.title: Refutation of the Bayer-Diaconis-McGrath conjecture for the riffle shuffle card guessing game with feedback
sources.snippet: A thesis record says the conjectured strategy is optimal for a single riffle but not in general.
sources.note: Third independent paper on the game. The optimal-for-one-riffle-only point rests on this single result, so the page calls its multi-riffle guesser a heuristic.

sources.title: Faro shuffle
sources.snippet: The article describes perfect in- and out-shuffles and notes that eight out-shuffles restore a 52-card deck.
sources.note: Establishes the order-8 fact. Result text only; the host cannot be fetched from here.

sources.title: Diaconis Graham Kantor Perfect Shuffles
sources.snippet: A course copy of the 1983 paper on the group generated by perfect in- and out-shuffles.
sources.note: Primary reference for perfect shuffles. Not opened.

sources.title: By ALEX STONE
sources.snippet: A review of a book on magical mathematics states that eight perfect shuffles return a 52-card deck to its original order.
sources.note: Independent confirmation of the order-8 fact; the scout's own permutation recount gives 8 for the out-shuffle and 52 for the in-shuffle. Not opened.

sources.title: wiki.dominionstrategy.com
sources.snippet: The community wiki says a reshuffle turns over the discard pile and shuffles it to form the new draw deck.
sources.note: Single source for the board-game deckbuilder rule; used as context only. Unverified.

facts.claim: About seven riffle shuffles are needed to mix a 52-card deck, measured by total variation distance (Bayer and Diaconis, 1992); with five or fewer, the original order is still plain to see.
After one riffle a deck has at most two rising sequences and the maximum roughly doubles with each further riffle, so five riffles cannot reach every arrangement of 52 cards.
Card guessing with complete feedback after a single riffle has been analysed by several independent authors, and an optimal strategy is known for one riffle.
Eight perfect out-shuffles restore a 52-card deck to its original order; the scout's recount also gives 52 for the in-shuffle.
As of 2026-10-11 the community wiki for a board-game deckbuilder describes a reshuffle as shuffling the discard pile into a new draw deck (single source, unverified).

design.coreLoop: A lazy dealer riffles a fresh deck k times (k hidden at first) and the visitor calls each next card from a tray of the unseen cards in original order, with every reveal acting as feedback. After the round the page shows hits against blind chance and a heads-tracking bot on the same shuffle, plus an exact likelihood table over k from the deck's rising-sequence count. A feint mode adds false shuffles and perfect faros to be called out, and a sweep plots the edge against the number of riffles beside the exact distance-from-random curve so the point where the edge dies is visible.
sophisticationHooks: Exact math in the page: the riffle law by rising-sequence count, 52-card total variation distance via Eulerian numbers in BigInt, and a posterior over the number of riffles after each round, all checked against enumeration for small decks
Seeded Monte Carlo edge curve (hits versus 1 to 10 riffles) in a worker with stated sample size and standard errors, drawn beside the exact distance curve
Bot honesty: an exact Bayes guesser for one riffle and a labelled heads-tracking heuristic for more, never described as optimal beyond one riffle
Feint mode: false shuffle and perfect faro (order 8 for 52 cards) versus real riffles, judged by the rising-sequence statistic; challenge links carry the seed in the URL hash
design.scopeForOneDay: In one morning the team builds: the riffle sampler and exact formulas with node self-checks (small-deck enumeration, the TV table, faro orders, known guess averages); the card tray and reveal UI with keyboard and touch; a canvas riffle animation; a worker for the edge curve; the round report with likelihood table; feint mode; an about panel with dated sources; hash state for seed and settings; light and dark; reduced motion. Cut: sound, overhand and pile shuffles, multiplayer, any deckbuilder clump panel if time is short, decks other than 52 and a 24-card phone mini deck.
risks: The seven-shuffles figure depends on the distance measure; a search summary mentioned another analysis with an information-based minimum near six shuffles, which is unconfirmed and not shown as fact. The page names total variation as its measure and plots the whole curve instead of declaring one magic number.

The riffle model is idealised; the claim that it fits real human shuffling is reported in the literature but rests on one unattributed search summary, so the page labels the model as idealised and shows that claim only as reported.
Calling cards among 52 on a 360px screen needs a compact tray design (rainbow-ordered tiles with unseen cards lit); a 24-card phone mini deck is the fallback.

Beyond one riffle the guesser is a heuristic, not a solver: its averages are computed by the page and labelled as such, and the literature suggests the best strategy is not settled in general (single result).
Framing: math and stage-magic lore only, with no money, chips, real casino or brand names; the false-shuffle content stays at the level of general knowledge about why order survives a shuffle.
Unverified items stay flagged: the Dominion-style reshuffle rule rests on one wiki result and appears as context only.
